1.pericope_label: Blessed is the man that feareth the Lord: his seed, his riches, and the light that rises in the darkness

schools.summary: Augustine takes the ascription of the psalm to two prophets of the Return as an invitation, since they foretold the restoration of the temple and whoever turns to that building understands the title.

Calvin notes the acrostic form and suggests one author for this psalm and the last, since the subject is only an enlargement of the closing verse of the other; Gill reads the wealth spiritually, of the unsearchable riches of Christ and a durable righteousness.

Henry observes that the words said of God in the preceding psalm are here said of the good man, so that we are to be followers of God as dear children; Spurgeon distinguishes a slavish fear which is accursed from a godly fear sweetened into filial love.

Clarke counts the acrostic exactly, reports the ascription to two prophets and a date after the captivity, argues from both languages that the righteousness meant is beneficence, and describes the discretion the good man uses in giving and lending; Wesley makes the righteousness the reward of righteousness in a blessed estate.

Ellicott derives the limited sense of righteousness from the parallel in the ninth verse and from rabbinical usage, and explains the strange construction of the fourth verse as a proverbial saying quoted without adjustment; Keil and Delitzsch pair the psalm with its predecessor and reject a rival construction of the same verse.

debates: What is the righteousness that endureth for ever? Ellicott holds that the parallel in the ninth verse requires the limited sense of liberality or beneficence which the rabbinical writings give the word, while allowing the wider sense to be true; Clarke reaches the same conclusion from the usage of both the Hebrew and the Greek; Wesley makes it the reward of righteousness in a blessed estate; Gill turns the whole verse to spiritual riches; Keil and Delitzsch make it the copy of the divine righteousness, which is by nature love.

Who is it that is gracious and full of compassion? Ellicott defends the received version in making the words describe the upright man, and explains the shift from plural to singular by supposing the first clause a proverbial saying quoted without adjustment; Keil and Delitzsch report and reject a construction that ties the epithets to the upright as a relative clause; Henry observes that the same words were said of God in the psalm before, so that the good man is a follower of God as a dear child.
outliers: Ellicott supports the endurance of goodness with a sentence from a novelist, that there is nothing, no nothing, innocent or good, that dies or is forgotten, and that we should hold to that faith or none.

Clarke describes the discretion of the good man in relieving others, that he takes heed both to whom he gives and to whom he lends, so that his bounty may be well applied and he may not oblige one who under the notion of a loan means to keep the money.
themes: fear of God sweetened into delight
a psalm answering the psalm before it
light rising in the dark for the upright

5.pericope_label: A good man sheweth favour and lendeth: the righteous in everlasting remembrance, unafraid of evil tidings

schools.summary: Henry divides the stability into a settled reputation and a settled spirit and prefers the second, and defines alms as righteousness because they are good deeds we are bound to perform, so that the uncharitable are unjust.
Gill derives the sense of a liberal man from usage in two languages, turns the promise of not being moved into a doctrine of perseverance, and divides the evil tidings between temporal and spiritual.

Clarke grounds the fearlessness in the knowledge that God governs the world and in a heart fixed to walk in duty; Wesley defines the discretion negatively and reduces the promise to a man afflicted but not destroyed.

Ellicott renders the opening word as prosperous rather than good and the closing clause as gaining a cause in the judgment rather than guiding affairs with discretion, and illustrates the fearlessness from the story of the man whose messengers of ill came one after another.

debates: Is the man of the fifth verse good or prosperous, and what does he guide? Ellicott holds that the word is not used in a moral sense but means prosperous, so that the line runs happy is the man who gives and lends, and would render the second clause that he will gain his cause in the judgment, as the old Greek and Latin apparently took it, or that he will sustain his affairs by justice; Gill derives from usage that a good man here is a munificent and liberal one; Wesley keeps the received clause and defines the discretion as neither getting an estate unjustly nor casting it away nor withholding it from the needy.

Why do evil tidings not frighten him? Ellicott offers the standing instance of the sufferer whose messengers of ill succeeded one another so fast, and adds that a good conscience is the best armour against fate; Clarke gives the reason instead, that the man knows God governs the world and has a heart fixed to walk in duty; Gill divides the tidings into temporal and spiritual and extends them to the trials of the churches in the latter day.
outliers: Henry defines alms as righteousness not because they justify by making atonement for evil deeds but because they are good deeds we are bound to perform, so that if we are not charitable we are not just, withholding good from those to whom it is due.
Ellicott sets against the fear of evil tidings the maxim that a good conscience before God is the best armour against fate, with a line from a play that virtue is bold and goodness never fearful.
themes: discretion in the use of an estate
a reputation that outlasts its owner
charity treated as a debt owed

8.pericope_label: His heart is established: he hath dispersed and given to the poor, and the wicked shall see it and be grieved

schools.summary: Spurgeon has the child of wrath compelled to witness the blessedness he cannot prevent, turns the gnashing into an image of frustrated malice, and holds that the wickedness by which the man hoped to succeed will itself defeat him.
Gill makes the established heart one settled in the teaching of grace and not tossed about, reads the scattering as a sower scattering seed, and keeps the beholder among ungodly men.

Clarke renders the heart as propped and buttressed, identifies the enduring righteousness with almsgiving, notes that the man rises to influence by worth and not by flattery, and observes that the beholder stands in the singular so that some take him for the adversary himself; Wesley holds that what a man gives is the only part of his estate that will abide with him for ever.
Ellicott notes that the form of the verb for scattering indicates a frequent and customary action, refers to the apostolic use of the verse, and glosses the melting away as consuming with vexation.

debates: What is the righteousness that endureth for ever in the ninth verse? Clarke says plainly that it is the man almsgiving and charity; Wesley calls it his liberality or the reward of it, and adds that what he gives is the only part of his estate which will abide with him to all eternity; Gill reads bounty distributed with wisdom and discretion; Ellicott notes only that the verb form marks a customary rather than a single action.

Who is it that sees and is grieved? Clarke observes that the word stands in the singular and is distinguished from the wicked in the plural at the close of the verse, so that some think the adversary himself is meant; Gill and Spurgeon keep to ungodly men, obliged to witness a blessedness they cannot prevent; Wesley divides the desire that perishes between the wish for the misery of good men and the wish for unbroken prosperity.
outliers: Wesley holds that what a man gives away is not lost but is indeed the only part of his estate which will abide with him to all eternity.
Spurgeon compares the melting away of the envious to a snail that melts as it proceeds and leaves a slimy trail behind it.
themes: a heart propped from outside itself
giving as a habit rather than an act
malice that can only grind its own teeth
a purpose defeated by its own means
